# MindCube: Spatial Mental Modeling from Limited Views. Full reference for LLMs and RAG tools

Paper: "MindCube: Spatial Mental Modeling from Limited Views", arXiv:2506.21458 (cs.AI), first submitted June 26, 2025 (v2: March 31, 2026).
Authors: Qineng Wang, Baiqiao Yin, Pingyue Zhang, Jianshu Zhang, Kangrui Wang, Zihan Wang, Jieyu Zhang, Keshigeyan Chandrasegaran, Han Liu, Ranjay Krishna, Saining Xie, Jiajun Wu, Li Fei-Fei, Manling Li.
Project page: https://mind-cube.github.io/
Challenge: https://mind-cube.github.io/challenge (CVinW Workshop @ CVPR 2026)
Code: https://github.com/mll-lab-nu/MindCube
Dataset: https://huggingface.co/datasets/MLL-Lab/MindCube

## What is MindCube?

MindCube is a benchmark that tests whether Vision-Language Models (VLMs) can imagine a full scene from just a few views, the way humans do. It contains 21,154 questions across 3,268 multi-view images. Existing VLMs exhibit near-random performance on it.

## What is a spatial mental model?

A spatial mental model is an internal representation of unseen space. Humans form them naturally to reason about layout, perspective, and motion: from a few glimpses of a room, people can answer what lies beyond the visible frame. MindCube measures whether VLMs build such representations from limited views.

## What is spatial reasoning from limited views?

Spatial reasoning is reasoning about the positions, orientations, and motion of objects in space. In the MindCube setting the model sees only a few views of a scene, so it must infer spatial relations it never directly observes, such as what lies to the left of an object when seen from a different viewpoint. MindCube frames this as spatial question answering over multi-view images, and shows that VLMs reason far better when they first construct an internal structured spatial representation (a cognitive map) and then reason over it.

## What abilities does MindCube test?

Three abilities, all from limited views: representing positions (cognitive mapping), orientations (perspective-taking), and dynamics (mental simulation for "what-if" movements). Questions are grounded in multi-view observations of real scenes, asking, for example, what is to the left of an object as seen from a different viewpoint.

## How do current VLMs perform?

Near-randomly. The benchmark exposes a critical gap between VLM spatial reasoning and human spatial mental modeling, covering both position and orientation reasoning and mental simulation of unseen viewpoints.

## What actually helps?

The "map-then-reason" approach: jointly train the model to first generate a cognitive map of the scene and then reason over it. This lifts accuracy from 37.8% to 57.8% (a gain of 20.0 points). Adding reinforcement learning on top pushes accuracy to 61.3% (a gain of 23.5 points over the baseline).

## What is the MindCube Challenge?

A challenge at the CVinW Workshop, CVPR 2026, built on the MindCube benchmark: spatial question answering from limited multi-view observations. Details: https://mind-cube.github.io/challenge

## Key numbers at a glance

- 21,154 questions; 3,268 multi-view images.
- Existing VLMs: near-random accuracy.
- Map-then-reason: 37.8% to 57.8% (+20.0).
- Map-then-reason + reinforcement learning: 61.3% (+23.5).
